versions.prompt:
Create a one-page 16:9 brand identity board that looks like a premium presentation artifact from an elite boutique design studio.

Inputs:
Company name: "tradelog"
Theme: "pastel_utility"
Brand description: "Same as co-founder. Keep it the same as you. We will keep the same vibe and all those things the way you are having this application."
Iteration notes: ""
Business context: <business_context>## Product or Service
TradeLog is a freemium SaaS trading journal and behavioral coaching platform built for retail forex traders. Core product loop:

1. **Auto-Sync from MT5** — Read-only MetaAPI integration captures every trade (pair, lot size, entry, exit, ₹ P&L) with zero manual entry.
2. **Rules Engine (Soft Block)** — Traders self-set discipline rules ("Max 3 trades/day", "No trading after ₹2,000 loss", "Minimum 1:2 RR"). When a rule is broken, the app surfaces a friction warning requiring a conscious override — preserving autonomy while creating accountability.
3. **AI Behavioral Insights** — Post-trade and weekly AI analysis (Claude API / Groq fallback) surfaces patterns the trader cannot see themselves: revenge trading frequency, session-time performance gaps, drawdown triggers.
4. **Voice-First Journal** — Traders speak their reasoning in Hindi/Marathi/English post-trade. Whisper transcribes and attaches to the trade for AI analysis. Audio is not stored.
5. **India-Native UX** — ₹-denominated P&L, UPI payments via Razorpay, Hindi/Marathi localization, Android-first.

**MVP Scope (v1 to Rich Royals):** MT5 auto-sync + rules engine + basic AI insights. Voice journal and advanced analytics are post-MVP.

**Tech Stack:** Next.js / TypeScript / Tailwind, Supabase (PostgreSQL + Auth), MetaAPI, Claude API, Whisper, Razorpay, Firebase, Vercel.

## ICP
**Primary (Launch):** Intermediate Indian retail forex trader
- 6–24 months of live trading experience on MT5
- Trades daily or near-daily, typically on a small account (₹10,000–₹1,00,000 capital)
- Knows the rules intellectually but breaks them emotionally — revenge trading, overleveraging, ignoring stop losses
- Based in Maharashtra or Hindi Belt; uses Android; pays via UPI
- Already part of or adjacent to the Rich Royals community (15,000+ alumni, 1,000+ active monthly traders)
- Willing to pay ₹299–499/month if the product demonstrably reduces costly emotional mistakes

**Secondary (Expansion):** Indian retail forex traders outside Rich Royals, reached via Telegram/Discord trading communities and Hindi/Marathi content.

**Tertiary (Scale):** Global retail forex traders on MT5 — same behavioral problem, different language and currency.

## Mission
Democratize professional trading discipline for retail traders globally — giving every retail trader access to the behavioral accountability and pattern recognition that professional traders have built into their workflows.

## Business Classification
- Company Type: SaaS startup
- Industry: Fintech / Trading Tools
- User Type: B2C (retail traders), with a future B2B2C layer (trading institutes / brokers)

## Company Values
- Discipline over motivation — build systems that work when emotions don't
- Radical transparency — show traders the uncomfortable truths about their own behavior
- Privacy by design — voice is transcribed, never stored; trader data is never sold
- India-first, globally minded — build for the underserved Indian market without capping global ambition
- Builders who trade — stay close to real traders; never build in a vacuum

## One Sentence Summary
TradeLog is an AI-powered trading journal for retail forex traders that auto-syncs trades from MetaTrader 5, enforces self-set discipline rules with friction-based blocks, and delivers personalized behavioral coaching — starting with India's Rich Royals community and expanding globally.</business_context>
Brand kit iteration history: <brand_kit_iterations>None yet.</brand_kit_iterations>

Use only these inputs. If details are sparse, infer a distinctive creative direction from the theme and notes. Do not render placeholders or missing-input text.

Iteration contract:
When prior brand-kit iterations are provided, treat their images and history as continuity context. Preserve the strongest approved direction, make the requested refinement intentional, and avoid accidentally reverting to an earlier rejected direction.

Creative standard:
This should feel expensive, authored, and specific. Avoid generic startup branding, basic design-system templates, Canva-style layouts, bland SaaS UI kits, and obvious moodboard grids.
The board should look like it was produced for a serious brand identity pitch: refined typography, intentional asymmetry, subtle tension, confident whitespace, precise spacing, elegant supporting details, and a memorable visual point of view.

Goal:
Produce a clean, inspectable identity board useful to a designer or frontend engineer. It should communicate the brand system through finished examples, not explanations.

Required sections:
"Brand Identity Board"
"Palette"
"Typography"
"Shape Language"
"Components"
"Art Direction"

Quality contract:
Every element must be high quality, including the canvas, section headers, dividers, annotations, art direction tiles, swatches, component examples, labels, and background structure.
All visible text must be crisp, readable, high-contrast, and intentionally placed.
Use short labels only. No tiny paragraphs, lorem ipsum, fake microcopy, pseudo text, or filler decoration.

Composition:
Use a sophisticated editorial layout, not an evenly spaced template grid. Create hierarchy with scale shifts, asymmetry, margins, rules, modular blocks, and negative space.
Make the board feel calm and inspectable, but not plain. Include one or two distinctive layout gestures derived from the brand direction.

Palette:
Derive 5-6 colors from the inputs. Use nuanced, professional color choices with clear hierarchy: foundation neutrals, primary accent, secondary accent, and one unexpected supporting color.
Show large swatches with readable names and hex values. Avoid default rainbow palettes.

Typography:
Show 2-3 type specimens that feel selected, not generic.
Include a display treatment, a practical UI/text treatment, and an optional technical or annotation treatment if appropriate.
Make typography visibly part of the first board through type specimens, role labels, scale, rhythm, and contrast.
Show concise font family labels when useful, paired with roles such as display, body/UI, and mono/annotation.
Do not show source names, foundry names, license notes, URLs, or implementation provenance on the board.
Do not make every specimen feel like the usual neutral startup sans-serif defaults; include at least one more ownable non-default type direction when it fits the brand.
Use short readable phrases that fit the brand. Make the type specimens beautiful enough to stand on their own.

Shape Language:
Show the brand's structural logic through finished visual samples: radius, spacing, dividers, panels, tabs, badges, status marks, crops, frames, overlays, or layout motifs.
These should feel like a proprietary system, not random rounded rectangles.

Components:
Show polished product or brand-interface examples such as buttons, segmented controls, inputs, chips, cards, navigation fragments, progress states, alerts, or dashboard tiles.
The components should inherit the brand's typography, color, spacing, and shape language. Avoid generic UI-library styling.

Art Direction:
Create 3-4 large art direction tiles with short readable labels.
Each tile should include a finished visual cue, not just text: image crop style, texture/material treatment, editorial layout crop, color behavior, motion/interaction hint, illustration style, or product-surface example.
These tiles should feel as designed as the main brand system.

Surface detail:
Use premium presentation details sparingly: small index numbers, fine rules, crop marks, alignment ticks, tasteful captions, soft paper texture, restrained shadows, or subtle material contrast.
Everything should support the identity system.

Avoid:
Basic brand-board templates, bland grids, generic SaaS dashboards, random decorative blobs, excessive gradients, stock-photo collage, mascots, 3D objects, nested cards, unreadable text, tiny notes, fake UI copy, overlapping elements, watermarks, existing brand logos.
